San Francisco

Alcatraz Island
Alcatraz rising out of the Bay on its own rocky outcrop, the old cellhouse and lighthouse catching the afternoon sun, the water tower still standing watch at the edge of the island.
Alcatraz operated as a federal penitentiary from 1934 to 1963, and the cold, fast currents ringing the island were part of what made it so hard to escape.
Powell & Hyde Cable Car Line
A tiny enamel cable car keychain, stamped Powell & Hyde Sts. and tagged San Francisco with a little Golden Gate Bridge charm, riding home as the trip's souvenir.
The Powell-Hyde line is one of only three surviving cable car lines in the city, and San Francisco's cable cars are the last manually operated ones left in the world.
Lombard Street
Looking down Lombard Street's famous switchbacks, hydrangeas banking every curve, with Coit Tower and the Bay stretching out beyond the rooftops.
Lombard's eight hairpin turns were added in 1922 to make the hill's natural 27-degree grade manageable for cars, with a posted speed limit of just 5 miles per hour.
Painted Ladies
A row of Victorian gables lined up along Alamo Square, downtown San Francisco's skyline rising behind them across the park's open lawn.
This row of Victorians, often called Postcard Row, was built in the early 1890s and survived the 1906 earthquake and fire that leveled much of the city.
Fisherman's Wharf
The big ship's-wheel sign marking Fisherman's Wharf, crowds gathering beneath it at the corner of Jefferson and Taylor.
Fisherman's Wharf takes its name from the Italian immigrant fishermen, many from Genoa and Sicily, who built up the district's fishing fleet starting in the late 1800s.
Golden Gate Bridge
The Golden Gate Bridge's near tower rising above the strait, a lone sailboat scattered across the water and the Marin headlands fading into haze beyond the far tower.
The bridge's signature color, International Orange, was chosen partly because it stands out against the Bay's frequent fog while still complementing the surrounding hills.
